text: Some questions can't be answered one row at a time. What's the three-day moving average of sales? How much did revenue change since yesterday? What's each customer's running total? These all need a row to look at its neighbors. In SQL you'd use window functions like average over order by, lag, and a running sum. pandas has direct equivalents, and this lesson covers them.

Here's one week of illustrative daily sales — a date column running for seven days, and a sales figure for each one. Important: every single operation in this lesson depends on row order. Sort by date first, and sort by date within each group whenever you're using groups later on.

Rolling of 3 builds a window of the current row and the two rows before it — follow it with an aggregation like mean. The first two rows come back NaN, because a full window of three doesn't exist yet. Check row three by hand: 120 plus 135 plus 110, divided by 3, comes to 121.67 — exactly what rolling computed.

If you'd rather get a partial result right from the start, pass min underscore periods equals 1, which averages whatever days are available instead of waiting for a full window. Add center equals True to place the window around each row instead of behind it — fine for smoothing a chart, but it leaks future information if you use it as a feature for a model. And for a date index, you can give the window an actual time span, like rolling of 3-D, which handles missing days gracefully.

Cumsum gives the running total from the very first row to the current one — 120, then 255, then 365, and so on through 940 by day seven. Cummax, cummin, and cumprod all work the same way for their own operations. And expanding dot mean gives a running average, where the window grows by one row each step but always starts from the very beginning.

Shift of 1 moves values down one row, so each row can see the previous row's value — it's the pandas version of LAG. Negative numbers look forward instead, like LEAD. Diff subtracts the previous row's value directly, and pct underscore change gives the relative change — day two came in 12.5 percent above day one, while day six fell 40 percent. The very first row has no previous value to compare against, so it's always NaN.

These methods become dramatically more powerful after groupby, because the calculation restarts fresh for each group. Sort the illustrative orders by customer and date, group by customer underscore id, then compute a running total per customer, the previous order's amount per customer, an order number starting at 1 using cumcount plus 1, and the days between each customer's orders using diff on the date. Customer 101's second order came 10 days after the first; customer 102 waited 62 days. Cumcount numbering plus 1 is exactly pandas' row underscore number over partition by — and time between orders, previous order value, and order number are all classic features for customer models.

To recap: rolling of n computes moving statistics, cumsum and expanding accumulate from the start, and shift, diff, and pct underscore change compare a row to its neighbors. Always sort first, and combine with groupby so the window resets cleanly for each customer or product. Next: working with text data.
